title: Higher energy prices weigh on APAC output while AI demand supports growth
gist: Oxford Economics holds APAC industrial production growth at 4.9% for 2026 but cuts 2027 to 4% (from 4.4%), as a prolonged US-Israel war with Iran drives higher oil prices and tighter monetary policy that hit energy-intensive and investment-reliant sectors. Stronger US AI data centre investment prompts another upgrade to electronics output, though concentration risk is rising as an AI investment slowdown looks more likely.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics kept its Asia Pacific industrial production growth forecast at 4.9% for 2026 but cut its 2027 forecast to 4% from 4.4% in August.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Signals a deceleration in APAC manufacturing output into 2027, relevant for regional cyclicals and commodity demand.
insights.quote: We have kept our industrial production forecast for the Asia Pacific (APAC) region at 4.9% in 2026
insights.locator: We have kept our industrial production

insights.claim: A more prolonged Middle East conflict is expected to weigh on APAC production through two channels: higher energy prices and tighter monetary policy.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Energy-shock-plus-hawkish-policy combo is the key downside driver for Asian industry next year.
insights.quote: We expect a more prolonged Middle East conflict to hit production via higher energy prices and tighter monetary policy.
insights.locator: We have kept our industrial production

insights.claim: Oxford Economics materially raised its oil price forecast for the next few quarters following the latest escalation in the US-Israel war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Higher near-term oil assumptions feed into inflation, rates and margin forecasts across energy importers.
insights.quote: We have materially raised our oil price forecast for the next few quarters
insights.locator: We have materially raised our oil

insights.claim: APAC is particularly vulnerable to higher energy prices because of its heavy reliance on Gulf hydrocarbons.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Asian energy importers are the most exposed economies to a Gulf supply shock.
insights.quote: Higher energy prices will hit APAC particularly hard, given the region’s heavy reliance on Gulf hydrocarbons.
insights.locator: We have materially raised our oil

insights.claim: Within APAC, petrochemicals, utilities and refining are the sectors most exposed to the energy price shock because hydrocarbons are a core input.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Points to sector-level underweights in Asian petrochemicals, utilities and refiners under the oil-shock scenario.
insights.quote: The exposure is greatest in petrochemicals, utilities, and refining, where hydrocarbons are a core input.
insights.locator: We have materially raised our oil

insights.claim: Higher energy prices and more hawkish central banks will further raise firms' financing costs at a time when global interest rates are already elevated.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Rising cost of capital pressures leveraged and capex-heavy companies.
insights.quote: Higher energy prices and more hawkish central banks will further raise firms’ financing costs
insights.locator: Higher energy prices and more hawkish

insights.claim: Narrow credit spreads and steady credit conditions are currently limiting overall financial stress despite higher rates.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Credit markets are not yet pricing stress, a potential complacency risk if the energy shock persists.
insights.quote: narrow credit spreads and steady credit conditions are limiting the overall financial stress level
insights.locator: Higher energy prices and more hawkish

insights.claim: Global investment growth is forecast to slow in 2026 before a modest pick-up in 2027.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Capex cycle trough expected this year, shaping timing for capital goods exposure.
insights.quote: global investment growth is set to slow this year before recording a modest pick-up in 2027
insights.locator: Higher energy prices and more hawkish

insights.claim: A stronger squeeze on investment demand will hit investment-reliant sectors such as machinery and construction in APAC.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Machinery and construction are the cyclical losers from the investment slowdown.
insights.quote: A stronger squeeze on investment demand will hit investment-reliant sectors such as machinery and construction.
insights.locator: Higher energy prices and more hawkish

insights.claim: Stronger-than-expected momentum in US AI data centre investment led Oxford Economics to upgrade its APAC electronics production forecasts again.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: AI capex remains the main offset to the energy drag for Asian tech hardware producers.
insights.quote: Stronger-than-expected momentum from US AI data centre investment has prompted us to upgrade our electronics production forecasts

insights.claim: APAC electronics export orders remain robust and production data continue to indicate steady output growth.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Hard data currently confirm the AI hardware upcycle in Asia.
insights.quote: Export orders remain robust, and production data continue to indicate steady growth in output.

insights.claim: China's government push to localise chip production adds a structural tailwind for its electronics sector on top of the cyclical AI boost.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Chinese chipmakers benefit from both policy-driven localisation and the AI cycle.
insights.quote: the government’s chip production localisation push provides additional structural tailwinds on top of a cyclical AI-related boost

insights.claim: Reliance on AI strength leaves APAC electronics exposed to concentration risk, and a slowdown in AI investment now looks more likely.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: The region's main growth support is itself fragile; an AI capex slowdown would remove the key offset to the energy shock.
insights.quote: AI strength leaves the sector vulnerable to concentration risks, especially because a slowdown in AI investment now looks more likely.
